questions.q: What is the dominant subject of this chapter's chorus of voices?
choices: Fear in the land, and the many clashing opinions about what to do about native crime
questions.explain: 'There are voices crying what must be done, a hundred, a thousand voices' — but 'one cries this, and one cries that.'

questions.q: What do the suburban public meetings mostly demand?
choices: More police, heavier sentences, and the death penalty for housebreakers who carry weapons
questions.explain: One speaker still argues the answer 'does not lie, except temporarily, in more police and more protection.'

questions.q: What figure does Mr de Villiers give for native schooling in Johannesburg?
choices: Nine in ten children are at school
Not more than four in ten are at school, and of those four not even one will reach the sixth standard
All children are at school by law
questions.explain: 'Six are being educated in the streets.'

questions.q: In the pass-laws argument, what does Jackson point out?
choices: The pass laws have ended crime
That about one hundred thousand natives are sent to prison every year, where they mix with real criminals
That passes are cheap and easy to get
That the laws only apply to men
questions.explain: He keeps insisting 'the pass-laws don't work' and are unenforceable, without a better answer of his own.

questions.q: How do the tennis-club women in the chapter propose to solve the problem of where black people can go on a Sunday?
choices: Open the Zoo Lake to everyone
Vaguely suggest big recreation centres 'somewhere' — but every specific site is objected to as too noisy or too far
Give servants the whole weekend off
questions.explain: 'It's too hot to argue' — they break off to play tennis.

questions.q: What does the narrator say 'we' will do to live with the fear?
choices: Put more locks on the doors, get a fierce dog, hold handbags tighter, and give up the beauty of the night
questions.explain: 'Our lives will shrink, but they shall be the lives of superior beings.'

questions.q: Why will the Cathedral Guild meeting on 'The Real Causes of Native Crime' have 'a gloom over it'?
choices: Its scheduled speaker, Arthur Jarvis, has just been shot dead
questions.explain: The irony: the man killed by native crime was the one about to speak on its causes.

questions.q: What news does Mrs Ndlela bring to Msimangu?
choices: That the police have been to her, looking for Absalom, and she gave them the Mkize address in Alexandra
questions.explain: 'It is the law, mother. We must uphold the law,' Msimangu tells her.

questions.q: What do Kumalo and Msimangu spend the chapter doing after Mrs Ndlela's visit?
choices: Chasing by taxi from address to address, always arriving just after the police who are hunting Absalom
questions.explain: Mkize sends them to Shanty Town, Hlatshwayo to the school, the reformatory to Pimville — 'now, now, that they left.'

questions.q: What phrase does the girl at Pimville say she overheard the police use?
choices: 'die spoor loop dood' — the trail runs dead
questions.explain: Kumalo, trembling in the taxi, says only 'I am cold, very cold.'
